conversation.content:
Hi there—I’m so glad we’re getting a chance to talk today. My name is Anna, and I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician. I’m here to check in on how you’re feeling since your baby arrived, because every new mom deserves support and a safe space to share what’s really going on inside.

We’ll use a short, well-trusted questionnaire called the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale—EPDS for short. It’s simply ten questions that help us see how your mood, energy, and thoughts have been over the past seven days. It isn’t a test, and there are no right or wrong answers; it just gives us a snapshot so we can figure out the best next steps for you. Everything you say stays completely confidential within your care team.

I’ll ask each question conversationally, and you can answer however feels most natural. When we’re done, we’ll go over what the score means and talk through any supports or resources that might help. Ready to start?

Over the past seven days, overall, have you still been able to enjoy things or look forward to events the way you usually would, or has that been harder lately?

Honestly? It’s been harder. Like, my sister wanted to take me out for coffee last week and I said yes, but the whole time I was just watching the clock, wishing I could go home and sleep. Even little things—music I used to like, or a show I’d binge—feel kind of flat. I still do them, but it’s like I’m going through the motions more than actually enjoying anything.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

Sometimes a little giggle slips out—like when the baby does that startled arm-flail in his sleep—but it feels shallow and it fades fast. Most of the day I’m too tired or worried to find much funny. So, no, I haven’t really been laughing the way I used to.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Not really. I keep telling myself I should be excited about little outings—like when my friend invited me to that stroller-walk group—but the night before I just lay there dreading it. Even planning a coffee run feels like one more chore. I still go, but it’s more because I “should” than because I actually look forward to anything.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… pretty often. If he won’t settle, I immediately think it must be something I ate or that I’m not holding him right. Yesterday he spit up a lot and I stood there crying, convinced I’d overfed him even though the nurse said it’s normal. I know in my head that babies just do these things, but the voice in my gut keeps saying, “You messed up again.”
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Yeah, that’s… that’s most of my day. I’ll be feeding him and suddenly my heart’s racing because I’m sure he’s not getting enough milk—even though the scale at the doctor’s said he’s gaining fine. Or I’ll lie down and start panicking that the ceiling fan’s going to fall on the crib. I know it sounds crazy when I say it out loud, but in the moment I can’t shake the fear until I check on him three or four times.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Yes. It hits out of nowhere—like last night I was just rocking the baby in the chair and suddenly I couldn’t catch my breath, my chest felt tight, and I was sure something awful was about to happen. I kept telling myself nothing was wrong, but for those few minutes I felt like I needed to run out of the room. It passed, but it keeps coming back at random times.
Things have been getting on top of me

Most days, yeah. It’s like the second I finish one feeding, I remember the laundry pile, then the dishes, then the texts I haven’t answered, and I feel this weight on my chest. I keep thinking, “If I just push through, it’ll get better,” but by evening I’m in tears because I never feel caught up. I’m not falling apart completely—I still get the bottles sterilized and the diapers changed—but it feels like I’m barely treading water the whole time.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Yes… I’ll lie down exhausted, but my head keeps spinning with all the “what-ifs” about the baby—Is he breathing? Did I fasten the swaddle right?—and I can’t settle. Then when I do drift off, I’m up again in an hour listening for every tiny grunt. By 3 a.m. I’m wide-awake, staring at the ceiling, feeling this heavy sadness I can’t explain.
I have felt sad or miserable

Yeah… most of the day, every day. It’s like there’s this gray cloud hanging over everything. I’ll be changing his diaper and suddenly feel like crying for no real reason. Things just feel heavy and joyless, even when nothing bad has happened.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Yeah… it’s been a few times this week. Yesterday I just sat on the couch, looking at the baby sleeping, and tears started rolling down. I couldn’t even tell you why—it’s like the sadness just spills over. It’s not every single day, but it’s definitely been more than usual.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No… I haven’t had thoughts like that. I feel overwhelmed and sad, but hurting myself hasn’t crossed my mind.

You've painted a very clear picture of how heavy life has felt since your baby arrived: the joy that used to come easily now feels remote, most days are clouded by sadness or worry, and even simple outings loom like chores. You're working so hard to keep everything running-feeding, changing, sterilizing-yet inside you feel as though you're barely treading water and often find yourself in tears. Night-time is especially tough, with racing thoughts about your baby's safety that keep you awake despite exhaustion.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 24, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient acknowledges occasional brief amusement but emphasizes that genuine laughter is rare and joy feels shallow, aligning best with 'definitely not so much now</sym>, <sym>Patient reports pervasive loss of anticipatory enjoyment and dreads planned activities, indicating "Hardly at all" level of looking forward to things.</sym>, <sym>Patient reports blaming herself "pretty often" with vivid, recent examples and persistent self-criticism, aligning with "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes pervasive, irrational worries that intrude throughout the day, matching 'Yes, very often</sym>, <sym>Patient describes sudden intense panic with physical symptoms and recurrent episodes, aligning with "Yes, quite a lot"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes frequent daily overwhelm and tears but still managing essential tasks, aligning with "sometimes I haven't been coping as well as usual"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes nightly inability to sleep due to intrusive worries and persistent low mood, matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports persistent daily sadness ('most of the day, every day') with tearfulness and pervasive joylessness, aligning with 'Yes, most of the time'.</sym>, <sym>Patient reports multiple crying episodes this week without clear cause, indicating "quite often" but not "most of the time"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** A score of 24 places well above the ≥14 threshold indicating probable major <med>peripartum depression</med> with co-occurring <med>anxiety</med> features. The patient endorses <sym>markedly diminished interest</sym> (Q1-2), <sym>constant self-blame</sym> (Q3), <sym>generalized anxiety</sym> and <sym>situational panic attacks</sym> (Q4-5), <sym>subjective overwhelm</sym> (Q6), <sym>sleep disturbance</sym> driven by low mood and rumination (Q7), and <sym>persistent sadness</sym> with frequent crying (Q8-9). No self-harm ideation is reported (Q10=0). These findings are consistent with <med>DSM-5 criteria for Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med>. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent appointment with <med>primary care physician</med> or <med>perinatal psychiatrist</med>
2. Discuss evidence-based treatment options including <med>psychotherapy</med> (CBT or interpersonal therapy) and consider <med>antidepressant medication</med> compatible with breastfeeding
3. Provide immediate <med>psychoeducation</med> about postpartum depression and anxiety to normalize symptoms and reduce self-blame
4. Recommend practical daily supports: split night-time duties if possible, 30-minutes rest breaks, reduced household expectations
5. Encourage safe <med>sleep hygiene</med> (dim lights, avoid screens during night feeds, brief breathing exercise when mind races)
6. Offer local support group information and 24/7 parent helpline numbers
7. Schedule follow-up EPDS within two weeks to monitor symptom trajectory and treatment response
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 24: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Summary  
Patient: Postpartum mother, infant age not specified  
Screening tool: Edinburgh Postpartum Depression Scale (EPDS) – 10-item self-report  
Responses obtained: 03 Jun 2025  

Symptoms endorsed (frequency/intensity):  
- Persistent low mood, joylessness, daily crying spells (Q8, Q9)  
- Marked loss of pleasure/interest; activities perceived as chores (Q1, Q2)  
- Excessive or inappropriate guilt; self-blame for infant-related events (Q3)  
- Generalized anxiety, situational panic attacks with physical symptoms (tight chest, breathlessness) (Q4, Q5)  
- Subjective feeling of being overwhelmed, “treading water,” difficulty completing daily tasks (Q6)  
- Mood-related insomnia (rumination, hypervigilance re infant safety) (Q7)  

Areas of screening significance  
- Score pattern consistent with probable major depressive symptoms (≥5 items indicating pervasive sadness, anhedonia, guilt, fatigue, sleep disturbance)  
- Co-occurring anxiety symptoms approaching panic-level intensity  
- Functional impact: impaired caretaking confidence, avoidance of social interaction, disrupted sleep despite exhaustion  

Safety items  
- Self-harm ideation: denied (Q10 = 0) – no current acute risk reported  

Risk factors identified  
- Primiparous adjustment challenges  
- High self-expectations/perfectionism (evidenced by guilt cognitions)  
- Limited perceived support (“should” statements, lone caretaking)  

Screening observation  
Patient demonstrates multiple depressive and anxiety symptoms of at least moderate severity that emerged post-delivery, exceed typical “baby blues” duration, and interfere with daily functioning. No self-harm thoughts at present. Recommend referral for comprehensive clinical evaluation (diagnostic interview, depression and anxiety measures), psychoeducation, and discussion of evidence-based treatments (therapy, medication options) as indicated.
